abstract: Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are central cell-cycle regulators that have undergone diversification in land plants; however, the functional implications of this divergence remain incompletely understood, particularly in non-vascular lineages. Here, we systematically dissected the roles of the three principal cyclin classes--D, A, and B--in the model moss Physcomitrium patens. We show that CYCD2 exhibits constitutive expression throughout the cell cycle, CYCA2 is degraded during mitosis and transcriptionally activated post-mitotically, whereas CYCB1 is M-phase-specific and rapidly depleted at anaphase. Overexpression and loss-of-function analyses revealed functional divergence among these classes: cyclin D primarily governs cell cycle entry and vegetative growth; cyclin B regulates mitotic progression with its overexpression causing division failure and arresting gametophore development; cyclin A regulates S-to-G2/M transition and exhibits overlapping functions with both D- and B-type cyclins, contributing to vegetative growth, mitotic fidelity, and gametophore development. Yeast two-hybrid assays showed that CYCB2 associates broadly with both CDKAs and CDKBs, CYCA2 preferentially interacts with CDKAs, and CYCD1 binds CDKAs along with a subset of CDKBs. Collectively, our results reveal both overlapping and class-specific contributions of D-, A-, and B-type cyclins to cell-cycle progression and development in P. patens, and suggest that complex tissues (gametophores) are particularly vulnerable to mitotic cyclin dysfunction. These findings provide a foundation for understanding how cyclin diversification underpins developmental plasticity across different contexts in non-vascular land plants.
